due to the significant difference in atomic arrangement between the amorphous interface and the FCC structure of Cu, a potential barrier forms, preventing dislocations from crossing the amorphous interface. This leads to dislocation pile-up at the interface, causing severe stress concentration.

The applied electric field accelerates processes such as dislocation slip, reaction, and annihilation, resulting in extensive dislocation annihilation within the interface and a more uniform stress distribution at the interface.
Both locking structures play identical roles, enhancing the work hardening ability through the pinning effect of the central dislocations.
